title: Union Minister of Jal Shakti Shri C. R. Patil Chairs 19th Meeting of Ganga Flood Control Board in New Delhi
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                29 OCT 2026 12:53PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The 19th Meeting of the Ganga Flood Control Board (GFCB) was held at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi on 27th October 2026 under the chairmanship of Union Minister of Jal Shakti, Shri C. R. Patil. The meeting was attended by Shri Suvendu Adhikari, Chief Minister of West Bengal; Shri Ram Nath Thakur, Minister of State for Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, Government of India; Prof. K. V. Raju, Member, NITI Aayog ; Shri Vijay Kumar Choudhary, Deputy Chief Minister of Bihar and Minister for Water Resources, Government of Bihar; Shri Swatantra Dev Singh, Minister for Jal Shakti, Government of Uttar Pradesh; representatives of the Ganga Basin States; senior officials of the Central and State Governments; and representatives of the concerned agencies.
The Ganga Flood Control Board (GFCB) was constituted by the Government of India on 18 April 1972 to facilitate coordinated planning and implementation of measures to address flood, erosion and drainage problems in the Ganga Basin. The Board is chaired by the Union Minister of Jal Shakti and comprises representatives of the concerned Central Ministries and Chief Ministers of the Ganga Basin States or their representatives, with the Chairman, Ganga Flood Control Commission (GFCC), serving as its Member Secretary. It provides a high-level institutional platform for strengthening Centre–State cooperation and coordinated flood management across the Ganga Basin. The meeting provided an opportunity to review ongoing initiatives, strengthen interstate coordination and deliberate upon emerging approaches for effective flood management.
During the meeting, the Union Minister of Jal Shakti launched the Punah Bharan Mobile App, developed by the Bhaskaracharya National Institute for Space Applications and Geo-informatics in collaboration with the National Water Mission. The application aims to facilitate scientific identification of suitable locations for artificial groundwater recharge interventions.
The Board deliberated on the revised mandate and restructuring of the Ganga Flood Control Commission (GFCC), which includes strengthening basin-level flood management planning, appraisal of flood management schemes, river morphology and sedimentation studies, and development of a Flood Management Information System (FMIS). The revised institutional arrangements are expected to improve coordination, technical appraisal and timely decision making.
The discussions also focused on preparation of risk-based basin Master Plans, assessment of the adequacy of waterways and ventways under bridges, improving the quality of Detailed Project Reports (DPRs), timely implementation of flood management projects and application of modern technologies in flood management.
Emphasis was laid on strengthening coordination among Central Ministries, State Governments and other stakeholders, particularly in addressing issues relating to river morphology, drainage congestion, infrastructure development and flood resilience. The importance of modern survey techniques, sound technical investigations, appropriate statutory clearances and timely resolution of project implementation bottlenecks was also highlighted.
The meeting reaffirmed the importance of an integrated, risk-informed and technology-enabled approach to flood management, supported by effective Centre–State cooperation, improved technical standards and coordinated implementation of flood management measures across the Ganga Basin.

Speaking on the occasion, Dr. Chandra Bhushan Kumar, Secretary, MoLE said that the Mela reflects the Ministry’s commitment to empowering PwDs through skill development, dignity of labour and economic independence. title: India Leads Globally with Green Hydrogen Offtake Commitments Exceeding 5.5 Lakh MTPA Till October 2026
subtitle: Indian Companies Sign 18 New Green Hydrogen Offtake Agreements for Over 4 Lakh MTPA in 2026
ministry: Ministry of New and Renewable Energy
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                29 OCT 2026 12:54PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Till October 2026, Indian companies have signed the world's largest Green Hydrogen offtake commitments - totalling over 5.5 lakh MTPA -positioning India as the global leader in Green Hydrogen supply commitments.
In the year 2026, Indian companies signed new 18 offtake agreements for the supply of over 4 lakh MTPA of Green Hydrogen equivalent quantity.
Since the launch of the National Green Hydrogen Mission in 2023, altogether 23 offtake contracts covering about 5.5 lakh MTPA of Green Hydrogen equivalent have been signed, out of which over 70% are earmarked for exports.
These Green Hydrogen projects are expected to attract total investments of around ₹90,000 crore (approximately USD 9.5 billion).
Indian suppliers are offering the world's most competitive prices for Green Ammonia and Green Methanol, strengthening India's leading position in European and Japanese markets.
Green Ammonia are emerging as clean bunkering fuel for the global and methanol shipping sector.
Green Ammonia is also being deployed for ammonia co-firing in thermal power plants to reduce carbon emissions.
Worldwide Green Hydrogen derivatives are increasingly being adopted in fertilizer production and refining sector to enable industrial decarbonisation.
As of October 2026, total Green Hydrogen offtake firm and signed commitments by India companies have reached 5,55,610 MTPA. This accounts to approximately 11% of the National Green Hydrogen Mission’s target. This makes India a Global Leader in Green Hydrogen space.
Fulfilling these comprehensive domestic and international agreements would require aggregate capital investment exceeding ₹90,000 Crore (approximately USD 9.5 Billion).
The
National Green Hydrogen Mission (NGHM) was approved by the Cabinet with an initial outlay of ₹19,744 crore up to the year 2029-30. The objective of the Mission by 2030 is to produce at least 5 Million Metric Tonnes per Annum (MMTPA) of Green Hydrogen. Further, the expected outcomes of the Mission include RE capacity addition of 125 GW, over Rs. 8 lakh crores in total investments, creation of over 6 lakh full-time jobs and aversion of 50 MMT per annum of CO2 emissions.
Indian enterprises have forged vital strategic partnerships and binding Green Hydrogen offtake agreements spanning major global markets. Notable contracts include:
ACME Group, India has signed an offtake agreement for the supply of 4,88,000 Metric Tonnes per Annum (MTPA) of Green Ammonia with IHI, Japan.
ACME Group has also signed an agreement for the supply of 1,00,000 MTPA of Green Methanol to Mitsubishi Gas Chemical (MGC), Japan.
L&T and ITOCHU have formed a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) for the supply of 3,00,000 TPA of Green Ammonia, with deliveries expected to commence from December 2029.
Reliance Industries Limited (RIL) has entered into a long-term Supply and Purchase Agreement with Samsung C&T Corporation, South Korea, valued at over USD 3 billion, making it one of the largest Green Ammonia off take contracts globally. Deliveries under this agreement are expected to begin by 2028.
Agastya is in the process of offtake for the supply of 2,50,000 MTPA of Green Methanol to SAR, Sri Lanka.
AM Green has been selected as the sole winner of the Asian lot in the H2Global auction run by HINT.CO GmbH, securing a long-term purchase agreement for the supply of Renewable Fuels of Non-Biological Origin (RFNBO) ammonia to Germany. Under this agreement, Hintco will purchase ammonia from AM Green for a minimum value of EUR 585 million over a period of 10 years. The first deliveries to Germany are expected in 2029.
AM Green has also signed a firm off-take agreement with Uniper, Germany for the supply of 2,50,000 MTPA of Green Ammonia
AM Green signed a binding head of agreement with Japan's major power producer JERA for the long-term supply of 70,000 MTPA of green ammonia.
Jouno Joules has signed an offtake agreement with Select Energy GmbH for 600 TPD (about 2,19,000 MTPA) of Green Ammonia.
Alongside export metrics, substantial domestic demand has been solidified under targeted government frameworks:
Under the Strategic Interventions for Green Hydrogen Transition (SIGHT) Programme of the Mission, agreements have been signed for the production and supply of 6,70,000 MTPA of Green Ammonia to 11 Fertilizer units spread across the country.
Similarly, under the SIGHT Programme, projects have been awarded for the production and supply of 30,000 MTPA of Green Hydrogen to the refineries of IOCL, BPCL, HPCL and NRL.

title: ‘ESTIC 2026’ Concludes with a call by Dr Jitendra Singh for transformation through technology;
subtitle:
Dr Jitendra Singh reaffirms PM Sh Narendra Modi’s advice to work on  Measurable Outcomes for Viksit Bharat 2047:

Union Minister Calls for Indigenous Research, Stronger Industry-Academia Collaboration and Time-Bound Translation of Technologies into Societal Solutions

Two Landmark Documents Released: National Vision for Science, Technology and Innovation and India’s STI Outlook 2026

Minister Emphasises Capacity Building, Emerging Technologies and a Stronger Link Between Scientific Institutions, Industry and Society

ESTIC to Evolve into a Global Platform for Scientific Excellence, Innovation and Technology-Led Transformation
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                29 OCT 2026 7:13PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Addressing the valedictory session of the “Emerging Science, Technology and Innovation Conclave” (ESTIC), 2026, at Bharat Mandapam here today, Union Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Science & Technology and Earth Sciences, and Minister of State in the Prime Minister’s Office, Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions, Atomic Energy and Space, Dr Jitendra Singh called for  transformation through technology. He also reaffirmed PM Sh Narendra Modi’s advice to work on  measurable outcomes for Viksit Bharat 2047.
Emphasising the need to move beyond scientific discoveries towards their practical application, the Minister said that the success of India’s research and innovation ecosystem must increasingly be assessed through its tangible contributions to national development and the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047. Building on Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s vision of outcome-oriented science and technology, Dr. Jitendra Singh emphasised the importance of identifying clear, measurable targets for the next three years to assess the country’s progress and strengthen its long-term scientific and technological capabilities.
The valedictory session was attended by Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India, Prof. Ajay K. Sood; Secretary, Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR) and Director General, Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), Dr. (Mrs.) N. Kalaiselvi; Secretary, Department of Biotechnology (DBT), Dr. Rajesh S. Gokhale; Secretary, Department of Science and Technology (DST), Prof. Umesh V. Waghmare; Secretary, Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES), Dr. Srinivasa Kumar Tummala; and Secretary, Department of Agricultural Research and Education (DARE) and Director General, Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR), Dr. Mangi Lal Jat, besides scientists, senior officials, industry representatives, startups and other stakeholders. The session featured presentations on key recommendations emerging from ESTIC 2026, followed by the release of two landmark documents and the valedictory address by Union Minister Dr. Jitendra Singh.
Dr. Jitendra Singh said that ESTIC must progressively evolve into a globally recognised scientific platform where researchers, academicians and innovators actively seek opportunities to participate, reflecting the quality and credibility of its scientific programme. Commending the organisers for bringing together a wide range of scientific disciplines and international experts, including Nobel laureates, he stressed that India’s research priorities must increasingly focus on indigenous resources, indigenous methodologies and technologies developed within the country. He also emphasised the importance of strengthening capacity building in science administration, enabling scientists and researchers entrusted with institutional leadership to develop the managerial and administrative capabilities required to guide scientific organisations effectively.
The Minister said that emerging areas of science and technology offer opportunities to accelerate India’s technological progress and improve the quality of life of its citizens. Referring to developments in biotechnology, genomics and space research, he emphasised the need to anticipate future scientific requirements, including space medicine, as human space missions become more complex and prolonged. He also drew attention to the wider applications of nuclear science and technology, including nuclear medicine, and stressed that their potential extends well beyond energy and strategic applications to healthcare and other societal needs. Dr. Jitendra Singh further emphasised the strategic importance of ocean science and the blue economy in shaping India’s future economic and geopolitical position, while calling for affordable and accessible nutrition to remain a national priority.
Dr. Jitendra Singh also congratulated the startup award winners and certificate recipients at the valedictory session. Referring to the Prime Minister’s interaction with startups during the inaugural day, he emphasised the need for deeper engagement among academia, research institutions, industry and emerging enterprises. He said that the discussions and recommendations emerging from ESTIC should contribute to a more integrated innovation ecosystem, with greater emphasis on developing technologies, facilitating their adoption and advancing India’s scientific capabilities towards the targets of Viksit Bharat 2047.
Earlier, Principal Scientific Adviser Prof. Ajay K. Sood said that the central objective of scientific research must be to move beyond discoveries and develop solutions that address real-world challenges. He emphasised stronger collaboration among government departments, universities, industry and local communities, along with more effective support systems for innovation. He also presented the two landmark knowledge documents prepared through inter-ministerial collaboration and a whole-of-government approach.
The National Vision Document for ESTIC 2026 brings together the long-term science, technology and innovation priorities of 12 ministries and departments across 12 thematic areas aligned with Viksit Bharat 2047. The India: Science, Technology and Innovation Outlook 2026 provide a comprehensive, evidence-based account of India’s evolving science, technology and innovation ecosystem, with quantifiable information intended to support policymaking and strengthen engagement with international partners. The STI Outlook is envisaged as a dynamic resource that will be updated annually.
Dr. (Mrs.) N. Kalaiselvi, Secretary, DSIR, and Director General, CSIR, presented the key takeaways from the session on advanced manufacturing. The discussions emphasised the need to expand the contribution of advanced manufacturing to India’s economy, accelerate the transition of successful technologies from development to deployment, and extend scientific and technological solutions to rural and underserved communities. Participants called for stronger collaboration between research laboratories and industry, common performance indicators for researchers and industrial partners, greater exploration of conventional materials for advanced applications, and capacity building in specialised manufacturing tools and technologies. The session also stressed the importance of translating indigenous research into solutions that generate measurable economic and societal benefits.
The Secretary, Ministry of Earth Sciences, outlined the recommendations emerging from the session on ocean science and maritime technologies. The discussions called for strengthening ocean observation systems through satellites, research vessels, buoys and autonomous platforms, supported by advanced modelling and artificial intelligence, to convert scientific observations into actionable ocean intelligence. The session emphasised bridging the gap between research and operational applications in maritime safety, weather and climate services, coastal protection, fisheries and strategic maritime capabilities. It also called for wider deployment of indigenous technologies in underwater robotics, deep-sea exploration, ocean energy and desalination, alongside stronger industry collaboration, accessible data systems, international cooperation and sustainable management of marine resources. The recommendations placed coastal communities and the sustainable development of the blue economy at the centre of India’s ocean science priorities.
The Secretary, Department of Biotechnology, presented the key recommendations from the session on systems and synthetic biology. The discussions focused on integrating systems biology, synthetic biology and artificial intelligence to improve biological research, experimental design and predictive capabilities. Participants emphasised strengthening shared research infrastructure by connecting bio-AI hubs, bio-foundries and biomanufacturing facilities, while improving process development, scale-up and reproducible testing. The session also called for developing a skilled workforce in engineering biology through interdisciplinary education and practical training, and for stronger academia-industry partnerships with clearly defined milestones to improve the scalability, affordability and industrial adoption of biotechnology solutions. The discussions explored the potential of biotechnology to address challenges in healthcare, agriculture, energy and the environment.
The Secretary, Department of Science and Technology, outlined the outcomes of the session on autonomous systems, physical artificial intelligence and robotics. The recommendations focused on strengthening the 25 technology hubs established under the National Mission on Interdisciplinary Cyber-Physical Systems, particularly in preparation for the Mission’s next phase beginning in January 2028. The session called for stronger testbeds connecting researchers and industry, the development of India-specific datasets, and closer collaboration among academic institutions, startups and industrial partners. It also emphasised patient capital for indigenous hardware, multidisciplinary hands-on training, safety-by-design principles, early customer engagement and viable business models. The draft vision envisages validation of pilot technologies by 2030, wider deployment and manufacturing by 2035, and global competitiveness in these technologies by 2047.
The Director General, Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR), presented the takeaways from the session on agri-tech, food systems and nutrition. The discussions emphasised an integrated approach to the agri-food system, bringing together multiple ministries, departments, research institutions and industry stakeholders. Participants called for unlocking the potential of gene-bank resources to develop nutritious and climate-resilient crop varieties, accelerating the application of frontier sciences such as genome editing, and strengthening collaboration between agricultural and medical research. The session also emphasised the need for appropriate regulatory frameworks, particularly for public-private partnerships, greater international cooperation through South-South learning, and enhanced human-capital development across the agri-food value chain. A theory-of-change approach was proposed to define the contributions of different departments towards a more sustainable, affordable and accessible food and nutrition ecosystem.
The valedictory session reaffirmed ESTIC 2026’s emphasis on strengthening India’s science, technology and innovation ecosystem through coordinated action across ministries, scientific institutions, industry and academia. With its recommendations spanning advanced manufacturing, ocean science and maritime technologies, biotechnology, autonomous systems, robotics, agriculture and nutrition, the conclave provided a platform for identifying priority areas for future research, technological development and deployment. The discussions also reinforced the need to connect scientific excellence with industrial adoption, national priorities and societal needs.
Dr. Jitendra Singh called upon the scientific community to carry forward the vision articulated by Prime Minister Narendra Modi and ensure that India’s scientific achievements translate into tangible outcomes for citizens, strengthen the country’s global leadership in science and technology, and contribute to the realisation of Viksit Bharat 2047.

title: DST’s ESTIC session discusses transformations in science and innovations with autonomous systems, physical AI and robotics
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                29 OCT 2026 12:16PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Eminent experts mulled over how Autonomous Systems, Physical AI and Robotics would change scientific research and technological innovations in the near future, in the session on Autonomous Systems, Physical AI and Robotics at the Emerging Science, Technology and Innovation Conclave (ESTIC) 2026 at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi.
Prof. Umesh V. Waghmare, Secretary, Department of Science and Technology (DST), said while inaugurating the session that, “Collaboration among industry, academia, researchers, start-ups and technology users is crucial to advancing autonomous systems, Physical Artificial Intelligence (AI) and robotics and translating scientific ideas into solutions with societal impact,”
He emphasised that synergy among users, academicians, researchers and industry representatives is essential for progress in these emerging technology areas. He said that their interaction is particularly important in translating research into practical applications that can benefit society.
Highlighting DST’s National Mission on Interdisciplinary Cyber-Physical Systems, Prof. Waghmare said that technology innovation hubs had been established at 25 leading academic institutions across the country. These hubs facilitate interaction between academia and industry and start-ups to help translate ideas from laboratories into the marketplace.
He noted that Phase I of the mission was scheduled to conclude in December 2027. He added that the discussions and feedback from speakers and participants at the session would help inform the formulation of plans for the mission’s second phase.
The session featured a keynote address, invited talks and a panel discussion, bringing together perspectives from industry, academia, research institutions and start-ups. Prof. Waghmare encouraged active participation and discussion to draw on the experience and insights of the different stakeholders.
Speaking during the session, Prof. Abhay Karandikar, Member, NITI Aayog, said that Physical AI is not merely an artificial intelligence challenge but also a systems engineering challenge. He emphasised that the successful functioning of intelligent physical systems depends on several interconnected components, including reliable sensors, efficient actuators, real-time computing, robust control algorithms, low-latency communication and energy-efficient hardware.
Prof. Karandikar observed that physical AI systems differ from conversational AI tools because errors involving robots operating in factories or autonomous vehicles can have immediate physical consequences. He stressed that reliability, verification, safety, security and trustworthiness must therefore remain central to research and development in this field.
He pointed out that India has an opportunity to develop autonomous systems by building on its capabilities in systems engineering, electronics, manufacturing, embedded systems, design, telecommunications and software. Integrating intelligence and advanced algorithms into existing capabilities in robotics, autonomous vehicles and other cyber-physical systems could enable the development of more reliable, safe and trustworthy autonomous technologies.
Prof. Karandikar also highlighted the interdisciplinary nature of Physical AI, noting that progress would require collaboration among experts working on embedded systems, AI models and algorithms. He said that these collaborations would be important in addressing the significant research challenges in autonomous systems.
Referring to the possibility of a dedicated national initiative, Prof. Karandikar said that stakeholder consultations had considered the proposal for a Physical AI Mission. He suggested that the next phase of the National Mission on Interdisciplinary Cyber-Physical Systems could provide an opportunity to take up this area, building on the capabilities developed under the existing mission.
The session was part of ESTIC 2026, being held from October 27 to 29 at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi, bringing together stakeholders from science, technology, research and industry to deliberate on emerging technologies and innovation.
Other dignitaries who participated in Session 6 included: Shri Jalaj A. Dani, Chairman, Addverb Technologies Ltd.; Prof. P. Rajalakshmi, IIT Hyderabad; Shri Ashutosh Dutt Sharma, IIT Delhi; Dr. Rohan Paul, IIT Delhi; Prof. Santosh K. Vishvakarma, IIT Indore; Dr. Rohini Srivathsa, Microsoft India (former CTO); Prof. K. title: 8-Day Shilp Samagam Mela 2026 Concludes Successfully in Guwahati, Assam
subtitle:
Mela Empowers Traditional Artisans, Promotes Indigenous Crafts and Strengthens Livelihood Opportunities

High Visitor Footfall, BHARAT-TULIP Initiative, Dedicated Ministry Pavilion and Cultural Performances Highlight Grand Finale
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                29 OCT 2026 7:55PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The eight-day Shilp Samagam Mela 2026 organized at Farm Gate, Khanapara, Guwahati in the State of Assam, came to a successful conclusion, drawing widespread appreciation from visitors, local communities and participating artisans.
Organised by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, Government of India, the Mela provided a vibrant platform for traditional craftspeople to showcase their heritage, establish direct customer linkages and enhance their socio-economic self-reliance.
The Guwahati edition marked the second event in the Shilp Samagam Series for the financial year 2026–27, following the successful conclusion of the opening edition on October 19, in Mysuru, Karnataka.
A Senior Official in the Ministry said the eight-day event successfully achieved its core objectives of fostering entrepreneurship, expanding market reach, and providing sustainable livelihood opportunities for artisans belonging to target groups, including Scheduled Castes, Other Backward Classes, Safai Mitras, and Denotified Tribes.
A total of 75 artisans, including 31 women artisans, participated in the Guwahati Mela, offering visitors access to approximately 40 distinct varieties of handloom and handicraft products.
The displays featured regional craftsmanship from the North-Eastern States alongside traditional arts from across the nation, including Assamese Mekhela Chadar, cane and bamboo craft, block-printed fabrics, embroidery, leather craft, and handloom textiles.
Direct interaction with consumers enabled artisans to build prospective business relationships, gain valuable market feedback, and generate substantial direct sales income.
A major milestone of the Mela was the visit of Shri Sudhansh Pant, Secretary, Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment. He was accompanied by Shri Prabhat Tyagi, Chairman cum Managing Director of NSFDC (National Scheduled Castes Finance and Development Corporation) and senior officers of the three APEX Corporations.
During his comprehensive tour of the stalls and Ministry Pavilion, Shri Pant interacted with artisans to learn about their skills and market opportunities.
He noted that the initiative aligns with the vision of Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi guided by the doctrine of
‘Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas’,
creating concrete avenues for artisans to convert traditional craftsmanship into sustainable economic independence.
A key focus throughout the Mela was the promotion of BHARAT-TULIP (Traditional Artisans’ Upliftment Livelihood Programme), which facilitates market access for artisans through physical outlets and e-commerce platforms. By connecting traditional skills with modern consumer channels, the program strengthens market linkages and helps artisans expand their business presence.
The dedicated Ministry Pavilion served as a key hub for public outreach, using interactive LED displays to inform visitors about welfare, financial assistance, and skill development schemes managed by the Ministry’s three National Corporations namely National Scheduled Castes Finance and Development Corporation (NSFDC), National Backward Classes Finance and Development Corporation (NBCFDC) and National Safai Karamcharis Finance and Development Corporation (NSKFDC).
Daily cultural performances featuring traditional music and folk dances representing the North-Eastern region added significantly to the Mela’s public appeal. These cultural programs were livestreamed throughout the eight days to extend public engagement beyond the physical venue.
The Ministry Official stated that the enthusiastic response from the public and the strong commercial outcomes for participating artisans demonstrate the effectiveness of combining direct market access, public awareness, and cultural promotion. Through initiatives such as Shilp Samagam Mela, the Ministry continues to advance its commitment to empowering marginalized communities and preserving India’s rich handloom and handicraft heritage.

content:
At 34, Mr Mahesh Kumar’s
(name changed),
journey highlights how compassionate care and sustained rehabilitation helps individuals rebuild their lives, strengthen family relationships and move towards a future of dignity and renewed purpose. His journey also reflects how timely treatment and livelihood support can help individuals work towards recovery and rebuild family well-being.
Mr. Kumar, a resident of Yadagiri district in Karnataka, has taken important steps towards a healthier and more self-reliant life.
Before receiving support, Mr. Kumar worked as a farm labourer. Alcohol dependence affected his health and employment and contributed to difficulties within his family. With limited awareness of available treatment options and financial constraints, accessing appropriate care was challenging. His wife and two children also experienced financial uncertainty and emotional distress. Despite these challenges, he aspired to overcome alcohol dependence, establish a small business and provide a more stable future for his family.
Under the National Action Plan for Drug Demand Reduction (NAPDDR), Mr. Kumar received support at the Shri Vaishnavi District De-Addiction Centre (DDAC), Yadagiri. He underwent a 30-day residential rehabilitation programme that included medically supervised detoxification, health monitoring, psychiatric evaluation and psychological support. Individual counselling, group therapy and Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) meetings helped him strengthen his commitment to recovery and develop healthier coping strategies.
The Centre also provided yoga, meditation, recreational activities and life-skills development to support his overall well-being. Family counselling helped improve communication and rebuild relationships at home. Vocational training and livelihood guidance supported his goal of establishing a small business. Treatment, medicines, food, accommodation and training were provided free of cost, alongside aftercare and relapse-prevention support.
Mr. Kumar has remained alcohol-free for the past four months, according to the information provided by the centre, and has established a small tea shop near Yadagiri bus stand. The business generates an income of approximately ₹12,000 per month, helping him meet household expenses and provide greater financial stability for his family. His children have returned to school, and the family is moving forward with renewed confidence and hope.
The NAPDDR intervention, delivered through the Shri Vaishnavi District De-Addiction Centre, Yadagiri, demonstrates the value of combining treatment, counselling, family support and livelihood guidance.
Mr Kumar continues to attend monthly follow-up sessions at the DDAC and receives guidance to support his recovery and livelihood. Aftercare, peer-group interactions and relapse-prevention sessions has helped him remain focused on long-term well-being and self-reliance.

title: Additional Secretary, MoSJE Smt Mona K Khandhar Visits Government Drug Rehabilitation Centre, Raiwala, Uttarakhand
subtitle:
Centre Promotes Recovery with Care, Respect and Dignity

Promotes A Holistic, Dignity-Centred Approach Combining Medical Care, Counselling, Wellness Activities And Resident Participation
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                29 OCT 2026 5:03PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Government Drug Rehabilitation Centre at Raiwala, Uttarakhand, is promoting a holistic, dignity-centred approach to drug rehabilitation by combining medical care, professional counselling, structured daily routines and wellness activities to support residents on their journey towards recovery.
Additional Secretary, Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, Government of India, Smt Mona K Khandhar, visited the Centre, managed by the Society for Promotion of Youth and Masses (SPYM), and interacted with the residents to understand their experiences and learn about the rehabilitation programme being implemented at the facility.
During the visit, Smt Khandhar expressed her intention to engage with the Ministry of AYUSH to explore the integration of appropriate traditional wellness practices, including yoga and naturopathy, into drug rehabilitation programmes.
She said the experience at the Raiwala centre could serve as a starting point for exploring pilot projects in collaboration with the Ministry of AYUSH adding the proposed initiative could examine how yoga, meditation, naturopathy and other suitable wellness practices may complement evidence-based medical treatment and professional counselling under appropriate clinical supervision.
The Additional Secretary said the proposed projects would require structured planning, documentation and evaluation to assess the safety, acceptability and potential benefits of these interventions. Medical professionals, AYUSH practitioners, mental health experts, research institutions and rehabilitation specialists could contribute to developing suitable protocols and quality standards, she added.
Smt Khandhar said subject to the findings of such assessments and the approval of the concerned ministries, successful practices could be considered for adaptation at other government-supported drug rehabilitation Centres across the country.
She said recovery is a gradual process built through small but significant steps, including healthier routines, open communication, restored confidence and preparation for a return to family and community life.
The Addl Secretary said the experience at the Government Drug Rehabilitation Centre, Raiwala, offers an opportunity to examine how professional treatment, psychological support, appropriate wellness activities and compassionate care can work together to support recovery.
With careful documentation, scientific evaluation and institutional collaboration, the initiatives at Raiwala could contribute to wider learning on strengthening drug rehabilitation services across India, she added.
Smt Mona noted that every person deserves care, respect, patience and an opportunity to rebuild their life.
Ms. Mona Kandhar's heard residents' experiences and took note of the initiatives being undertaken at the Raiwala Centre.
Smt Khandhar underlined the importance of transparent institutional practices, qualified professionals, effective grievance-redressal systems and safeguards against abuse. Rehabilitation facilities must provide safe, professional and humane care, ensuring that individuals seeking treatment are protected from violence, intimidation and humiliation, she said.
Smt Khandhar proposed engagement with the Ministry of AYUSH that could open avenues for dialogue on integrating appropriate traditional wellness practices into rehabilitation services. Documenting the programme and evaluating selected interventions through carefully designed pilot projects could help the concerned ministries determine their suitability for wider application, she said.
She said such collaboration could also contribute to common guidelines, staff training, resident participation and quality standards, while ensuring that evidence-based medical care remains central to treatment.
Executive Director of Society for Promotion of Youth and Masses (SPYM) Dr. Rajesh Kumar said the residents shared their experiences of participating in daily activities and explained how structured routines, wellness practices and a supportive environment had become part of their recovery journey. He said the interaction highlighted the importance of addressing not only substance dependence but also the physical, psychological and social challenges associated with recovery.
Dr. Kumar informed that the Centre incorporates wellness activities such as Yoga, Yoga Nidra, Acupressure, Massage, Mud Therapy And Epsom Salt Therapy as part of its broader rehabilitation environment. These activities helped them manage stress, maintain healthier routines and improve their overall sense of well-being, the official said.
The Executive Director said these practices are intended to complement, rather than replace, appropriate medical treatment, professional counselling and clinically supervised withdrawal management adding their safety and effectiveness in supporting recovery would require systematic assessment and evaluation.
He said the approach seeks to address the overall well-being of residents by combining professional support with structured activities that encourage healthy habits, emotional resilience and renewed self-confidence.
Dr Kumar said at the Raiwala Centre, the residents are encouraged to participate in daily routines, share their concerns and contribute to group activities. He added that participation in maintaining their surroundings, supporting fellow residents and undertaking shared responsibilities helps foster a sense of belonging and mutual respect.
Executive Director said the residents are also encouraged to express their preferences regarding daily routines, food, menus and recreational activities. Shared meals and group interactions provide opportunities to build relationships and strengthen community bonds, he added.
The SPYM Official further said the approach recognizes that rehabilitation must be rooted in respect for individual dignity, patience and compassionate care. Giving residents a voice in their rehabilitation helps to create a supportive environment that encourages meaningful participation in the recovery process, he said.
The Raiwala centre's experience presents an opportunity to explore how medical treatment, counselling, wellness activities and resident participation can be brought together within a structured rehabilitation programme.
Further strengthening of such services could include individualized rehabilitation plans, regular resident feedback, confidential grievance-redressal mechanisms, greater family involvement, discharge planning, community reintegration and follow-up support after residents leave the facility. Training for staff in professional, compassionate and safe care would also be important.
Systematic monitoring and independent evaluation could help assess treatment engagement, psychological well-being and longer-term recovery outcomes. Such evidence would be essential before recommending wider adoption of particular wellness interventions or rehabilitation practices.

subtitle:
Union Tourism Minister Shri Gajendra Singh Shekhawat calls for transforming North East’s tourism potential into business opportunities and sustainable livelihood

Ministry of Tourism emphasises sustainable tourism, improved connectivity and livelihood opportunities for local communities

Domestic tourist visits to North Eastern States increase from 95.65 lakh in 2019 to 1.51 crore in 2025
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                29 OCT 2026 9:22PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The 14th edition of the International Tourism Mart (ITM), organised by the Ministry of Tourism, Government of India, in association with the Government of Arunachal Pradesh and other North Eastern States, commenced today at Tawang, Arunachal Pradesh. The three-day Mart, being held from 29 to 31 October 2026, aims to showcase the tourism potential of the eight North Eastern States and strengthen business engagement with domestic and international tourism markets.
The inaugural session was held in the presence of Shri Gajendra Singh Shekhawat, Union Minister for Tourism and Culture; Shri Suresh Gopi, Union Minister of State for Tourism and Petroleum & Natural Gas; Dr. Sukanta Majumdar, Union Minister of State for Education and Development of North Eastern Region (DoNER); Shri Pema Khandu, Chief Minister of Arunachal Pradesh; and Shri Prem Singh Tamang, Chief Minister of Sikkim. Tourism Ministers from the North Eastern States, senior officials of the Central and State Governments, international and domestic tourism stakeholders and representatives of the travel industry were also present. Addressing the inaugural session, Union Minister Shri Gajendra Singh Shekhawat emphasised that the International Tourism Mart has evolved beyond a promotional platform into an important avenue for tourism partnerships and business opportunities. He stated,
“
ITM is not merely a tourism marketplace; it is a platform for building partnerships, generating business opportunities and creating a shared vision for the growth of tourism in the North East Region.”
Highlighting the immense potential of the region, the Minister said that its rich biodiversity, cultural heritage, spiritual traditions and natural landscapes offer distinctive opportunities for adventure, nature-based and experiential tourism. He particularly emphasised the potential of adventure tourism, music festivals and concert tourism to attract new visitor segments, encourage longer stays and generate economic opportunities for local communities. He also called for developing tourism experiences with appropriate safety standards, community participation and environmental safeguards.
The Minister highlighted the Government
’
s continued focus on improving connectivity, tourism infrastructure and destination experiences in the North Eastern Region. He also underlined the Ministry
’
s support for tourism promotion through domestic and international travel fairs, festivals, digital platforms and familiarisation visits, along with skill development initiatives to create employment opportunities for local youth.
Earlier, addressing a press conference, Union Minister Shri Gajendra Singh Shekhawat highlighted that the 14th International Tourism Mart has brought together 43 international buyers from 22 countries, the highest-ever international buyer participation at ITM, along with 42 domestic buyers from 16 States and Union Territories and 81 sellers. He emphasised that hosting the Mart in Tawang would bring greater attention to lesser-known destinations in the North Eastern Region and showcase their tourism potential to domestic and international markets. Highlighting the growth of tourism in the region, he noted that domestic tourist visits to the eight North Eastern States increased from 95.65 lakh in 2019 to 1.51 crore in 2025, registering a growth of approximately 58%.
The Minister also highlighted the Government
’
s continued focus on strengthening tourism infrastructure and connectivity in the region. He informed that 16 projects worth ₹1,309 crore have been sanctioned under Swadesh Darshan 1.0, 17 projects worth ₹564 crore under Swadesh Darshan 2.0, nine projects worth ₹139 crore under Challenge Based Destination Development, nine projects worth ₹790 crore under SASCI and nine projects worth ₹258 crore under PRASHAD. Additionally, the Ministry has supported ten tourism routes in the North Eastern Region under the Regional Connectivity Scheme–UDAN. He reiterated the Government
’
s commitment to promoting sustainable tourism, improving visitor experiences and creating livelihood opportunities for local communities.
During the inaugural session, Union Minister of State for Tourism Shri Suresh Gopi highlighted the opportunities for developing innovative tourism products, including cultural, adventure, festival and community-based experiences. He also emphasised the importance of the Ministry
’
s initiatives, Dekho Apna Desh 2.0 and the National Digital Tourism Stack, in promoting lesser-known destinations and improving digital visibility and market access for local tourism service providers.
The inaugural session also featured addresses by Shri Pema Khandu, Chief Minister of Arunachal Pradesh; Shri Prem Singh Tamang, Chief Minister of Sikkim; and Dr. Sukanta Majumdar, Union Minister of State for Education and DoNER.
As part of the programme, the North East Bazaar was inaugurated, showcasing traditional handicrafts, handlooms and other cultural offerings of the region. A cultural programme highlighting the rich traditions of the North Eastern States was also organised.
The Mart will feature tourism presentations by all eight North Eastern States and structured B2B meetings. A Regional Meeting of Tourism Ministers of the North Eastern States will be held on 30 October 2026 to deliberate on tourism development, regional cooperation, tourist facilitation and emerging tourism opportunities.
The 14th edition marks the return of the International Tourism Mart to Tawang after 13 years, following the second edition held here in 2013. The event seeks to strengthen tourism partnerships, promote lesser-known destinations and position the North Eastern Region as a leading destination for sustainable and experience-based tourism.

In Mandsaur, Member of Parliament Shri Sudhir Gupta interacted with participants. In Narmadapuram, Member of Parliament Shri Darshan Singh Choudhary and Asian Games bronze medallist Harshita Tomar interacted with youth, highlighting the importance of voting rights and informed electoral participation.

The 23 programmes were held in Raipur, Chhattisgarh; Betul, Mandsaur and Narmadapuram in Madhya Pradesh; Sabarkantha (Himmatnagar) and Kutch (Bhuj) in Gujarat; Kupwara in Jammu and Kashmir; Ghaziabad, Shahjahanpur and Sultanpur in Uttar Pradesh; and Shekhpura in Bihar. title: Cloud Ecosystem in India
subtitle: Building the Digital Foundation for Secure and Scalable Computing
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                29 OCT 2026 2:04PM by PIB Delhi
content:
India’s rapid digitalisation is driving demand for secure, scalable and reliable cloud infrastructure. Cloud computing is becoming an important foundation for digital governance and public service delivery. India is building domestic cloud capabilities through initiatives such as MeghRaj and the expansion of indigenous data centre capacity. Policy measures, institutional mechanisms, and public-private collaborations further drive cloud adoption across sectors in India.
Seeding Cloud for Data Sovereignty
India’s digital transformation is generating unprecedented volumes of data across governance, commerce, communication and public services. The country’s
internet subscriber base reached 1,092.79 million
in March 2026. Rising digital adoption is also driving higher data consumption, with average wireless data usage reaching
25.51 GB per subscriber per month
. Total wireless data usage rose to
285,376 petabytes in FY 2025–26
. Digital payments generate transaction records, online public services create digital records, and artificial intelligence applications generate and process vast amounts of information.
Managing this growing data requires secure, scalable and reliable infrastructure to store, process and manage information efficiently.
Meeting these requirements demands more than storage space. Organisations also need computing power to process information, run applications and deliver digital services reliably. Maintaining physical servers and other equipment independently can be expensive and difficult to expand.
Cloud computing addresses this challenge by providing computing resources over the internet, whenever required.
However, as dependence on cloud services grows, protecting sensitive information and maintaining control over its storage and processing become increasingly important.
Developing a domestic cloud can support data sovereignty by strengthening national control over critical digital resources.
Cloud computing
enables users to access computing resources, including data storage, servers, software and processing capabilities, over the internet. Instead of purchasing and maintaining their own servers, organisations can use these resources as needed.
For example, Google Drive allows users to store documents online and access them across multiple devices
. Similarly,
a government department can host its applications and databases on a cloud platform instead of maintaining all the necessary equipment itself
. When backed by appropriate security safeguards and governance frameworks, domestic cloud infrastructure can strengthen control over sensitive information. It can also support reliable public services, artificial intelligence development and India’s technological self-reliance.
India’s Cloud Service Provider Ecosystem
As of September 2026, India has empanelled 30 Cloud Service Providers (CSPs), with infrastructure across locations including but not limited to Mumbai, Navi Mumbai, Chennai, Hyderabad, Bengaluru, Delhi-NCR and Jamnagar. The empanelled providers include Indian companies such as Jio Platforms Limited, Tata Consultancy Services Limited, Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited (BSNL), ITI Limited, RailTel Corporation of India Limited, AdaniConneX Private Limited and Yotta Data Services Private Limited. International providers include Google Cloud India Private Limited, Oracle India Private Limited, Microsoft Corporation India Private Limited and Amazon Web Services India Private Limited, among others.
Key Benefits of Cloud Computing
Cloud computing offers several benefits by making digital infrastructure more accessible, flexible and efficient. It
reduces costs
by limiting the need to purchase and maintain physical servers.
A
server room
is a dedicated space housing computers that store data and run digital services. For example, a school can store student records on a cloud platform instead of investing in its own computing infrastructure.
It enables
faster deployment of digital services and applications
by letting organisations launch services without lengthy infrastructure setup. For instance, a hospital can introduce an online appointment system without setting up its own servers.
Cloud platforms also provide
easy scalability
, allowing organisations to adjust computing resources according to demand. For example, an online examination portal can increase its resources during registration periods and reduce them afterwards.
Cloud computing promotes
better collaboration
by allowing users in different locations to access and share information. For instance, university students can collaborate on research projects, share study materials and edit documents online
.
Cloud platforms reinforce
data backup and recovery
, helping users retrieve information after accidental deletion, equipment failure or other disruptions
.
For example, a hospital can restore backed-up patient records following a system failure.
These capabilities also strengthen
service continuity
by helping organisations resume operations quickly after unexpected interruptions
.
For example, an online banking service can switch to backup systems when its primary infrastructure encounters technical problems.
Cloud computing further supports
efficient data management
by simplifying the storage, organisation and retrieval of digital records. For instance, an e-commerce business can manage product information, customer orders and inventory records through a single cloud-based system.
Migration of Digital India BHASHINI Platform to the Cloud
The Digital India BHASHINI platform demonstrates how indigenous cloud infrastructure can support data sovereignty while improving digital services. In February 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology reported BHASHINI’s migration to an Indian cloud operated by Yotta Data Services. This transition keeps its language datasets, AI models and citizen interactions within India’s jurisdiction. The deployment reportedly
achieved up to 40% improved performance
,
20–30% cost savings and 99.99% uptime.
During Maha Kumbh 2025, BHASHINI supported real-time translation and voice-based assistance in more than 11 Indian languages. Its multilingual services helped pilgrims access information despite language barriers.
Creative Minds, Catalyzing Science, Empowering Technologies
ESTIC-2026, the second edition of India’s Emerging Science, Technology and Innovation Conclave, is being held from 27–29 October 2026 at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi. The conclave follows the theme
“Creative Minds, Catalyzing Science, Empowering Technologies.”
Organised by the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), ESTIC-2026 advances emerging scientific and technological frontiers, including
cloud computing
and other emerging technologies. It catalyses strategic collaborations and supports India’s vision of Viksit Bharat 2047. Spanning 12 thematic areas, the conclave features plenary sessions, technical discussions and exhibitions.
Click to Read More on Agenda:
ESTIC 2026
Understanding the Fundamentals of Cloud Computing
Types of Cloud Models
Cloud models determine
where cloud infrastructure operates, who can use it, and how much control an organisation retains
. The three commonly discussed models are public, private and hybrid cloud.
A
public cloud
uses infrastructure provided by a third-party provider and shared among multiple customers. For example, a business/video-streaming company serves millions of viewers from shared servers.
A
private cloud
dedicates infrastructure to a single organisation. For example, a state treasury office keeps payment and accounts data on a private cloud to manage sensitive administrative records with greater control over security.
A
hybrid cloud
combines public and private cloud environments. For example, a municipal corporation keeps its property-tax payment portal on a public cloud and citizens’ records on a private one. The choice depends on an organisation’s security, cost and operational requirements.
Various Cloud Services
Cloud services offer different levels of computing support, from renting digital infrastructure to using ready-made applications. Four common categories are
Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS), Platform as a Service (PaaS), Software as a Service (SaaS)
and
serverless computing
. These are also sometimes called the cloud computing "stack" because they build on top of one another.
Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)
allows users to rent computing resources such as virtual servers, storage and networks instead of buying physical equipment. For instance, an online retailer can lease cloud servers to host its website and scale computing capacity to accommodate surges in traffic during festive sales.
Platform as a Service (PaaS)
enables developers with tools to build, test and launch applications without managing the underlying infrastructure. For example, a team developing a mobile banking application can use a cloud platform to build and test its software.
Software as a Service (SaaS)
delivers ready-to-use software over the internet, with the provider managing updates and maintenance. Examples include
Zoom
for video conferencing,
Salesforce
for customer relationship management and
Dropbox
for online file storage and sharing.
Serverless computing
allows developers to run specific tasks without managing servers directly. The cloud provider manages the infrastructure and allocates resources when required. For example, an online shopping platform can automatically process an order when a customer completes a purchase. Despite its name, serverless computing still uses servers; the provider manages them on the developer’s behalf.
India’s Progress in the Deployment of Indigenous Cloud Ecosystem
India is reinforcing its domestic cloud ecosystem to aid digital governance, data management and emerging technologies. The Government is branching out shared infrastructure, implementing trusted cloud services and driving indigenous computing capabilities.
MeghRaj and MeghRaj 2.0: Government of India’s Cloud Ecosystem
MeghRaj,
the Government of India’s Cloud Ecosystem, was launched in 2014 by the MeitY to accelerate e-governance and optimize public ICT spending.
MeghRaj 2.0
represents the second-generation iteration of this National Cloud Computing Initiative, serving as the secure digital backbone for the country’s Digital India mission. By providing flexible IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS models through a distributed cloud architecture, it allows government departments to rapidly deploy digital applications on demand.
The ecosystem has scaled tremendously in the last decade. By September 2026, adoption grew to encompass 2,330 government departments. Today, MeghRaj 2.0 provides the highly secure, AI-ready hosting required to power India's digital platforms, including DigiLocker, MyGov, and the National Scholarship Portal, alongside the Department of Posts' Advanced Postal Technology (APT).
Click to Read More About: India Digital Public Infrastructure
Data Centres as a Pillar of India’s Cloud System
Data centres house the servers and storage systems that power cloud computing. India’s data centre sector is gaining momentum, driven by growing demand for digital services and AI computing. As of August 2026, India’s data centre capacity reached
1.57 GW
and is projected to grow to nearly
8 GW by 2030
. The sector is concentrated in Mumbai, Navi Mumbai, Chennai, Hyderabad, Bengaluru, Delhi-NCR and Jamnagar. Emerging data centre hubs are also gaining traction in Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and West Bengal
.
Meeting this growing demand requires substantial capital, and the sector is attracting around USD 70 billion in investments underway, alongside a further USD 90 billion in announced projects. These investments are expected to augment computing capacity and broaden India’s domestic cloud capabilities.
Click to Read More About: Data Centres In India
Strengthening the Data Centre Network
The National Informatics Centre (NIC) forms an integral part of India’s data centre infra, operating 4 National Data Centres and 24 Mini Data Centres across the country. These facilities provide shared hosting, co-location and cloud services to government departments. Mini data centres at NIC State Centres further cater to state-level e-governance requirements through decentralised yet standardised infrastructure.
IndiaAI Mission — Democratizing Access to AI Computing
Cloud infrastructure equips researchers and start-ups with the computing resources needed to deploy AI applications. The
IndiaAI Mission
, approved with an outlay of
₹
10,371.92 crore
, is broadening access to computing resources. More than
45,000 Graphics Processing Units (GPUs)
have been onboarded for a common AI computing facility. These resources provide Indian start-ups and academic institutions with affordable computing power for AI development, reducing the need for investment in dedicated equipment.
Click To Read More About: Transforming India with AI
Upskilling and Capacity Building Initiatives in Cloud Computing
Building a skilled workforce is essential to operating India’s expanding digital infrastructure. The FutureSkills PRIME Programme, launched in 2021 by MeitY–NASSCOM, promotes emerging-technology skills. By August 2026, it had 34 lakh registered candidates, with over 23 lakh enrolled or trained. It ranked 3rd globally in the European Commission’s Pact for Skills Report 2024 for industry-focused training in AI, cloud computing and data analytics. Complementing this initiative,
the
National Institute of Electronics and Information Technology (NIELIT)
operates 56 centres, 750 affiliated institutes and over 9,000 facilitation centres, training professionals in cloud computing, AI, cybersecurity, blockchain and IoT.
Further reflecting this talent base, a 2026 report by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) estimates that India has 2.25 million cloud-native developers. The report also finds that 44% of Indian developers use hybrid cloud, combining public and private cloud environments. This skilled workforce can facilitate the management of India’s evolving cloud ecosystem.
Policy Push Driving Cloud Adoption in India
India’s cloud strategy centres on building a globally competitive digital infrastructure through coordinated policy initiatives and targeted investments. Recognising cloud and data centres as critical to emerging technologies and data-driven services, the Union Budget 2026–27 highlighted their role in advancing India’s digital capabilities. The measures aim to attract investment in cloud computing, AI, and hyperscale data centres while enhancing India’s long-term digital capacity.
Did You Know?
In March 2026, MeitY issued a
Cloud Selection Framework
which provides structured guidance to Ministries and Departments for selecting cloud infrastructure based on data sensitivity and criticality. It introduces a data classification approach aligned with national security considerations, prioritises the use of government-backed cloud such as NIC and State Data Centres, and enables adoption of hybrid deployment models with empanelled cloud service providers.
Additionally, the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 establishes safeguards for personal data processing and sets conditions for cross-border data transfers. It encourages the use of local data centres and cloud services, as reflected in provisions related to
data residency and restrictions on cross-border data transfer
.  It also ensures better control over data and compliance with regulations through provisions on
explicit user consent, accountability of data fiduciaries, and strict data processing obligations
.
Guiding Secure and Standardised Digital Governance
The National e-Governance Division (NeGD) offers technical and advisory aid for e-governance projects at central and state levels. Its responsibilities include technical appraisal of projects, including their technology architecture, security, standards and use of common infrastructure. This collaborative framework is taking forward cloud services throughout India's government ecosystem, fuelling Digital India and e-Governance priorities.
The Path Forward for India’s Cloud Ecosystem
India’s cloud ecosystem is witnessing rapid expansion, with the country’s cloud data capacity projected to grow nearly 4–5 times by 2030. Rising reliance on cloud infrastructure across digital governance, public service delivery, and technology-driven platforms is driving demand for computing resources. Investments in data centres are augmenting domestic capacity, while targeted skill-development initiatives are cultivating a workforce equipped for cloud-based technologies. Together, these measures are fostering innovation and positioning cloud computing as a cornerstone of India’s long-term digital transformation.

title: Minimum Support Price for Rabi: Marketing Season 2027-28
subtitle: Strengthening Price Assurance, Procurement and Farmer Access
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                29 OCT 2026 11:06AM by PIB Delhi
content:
Minimum Support Price (MSP) serves as an important mechanism for providing price assurance to farmers and supporting informed decisions on agricultural planning and investment. On 30 September 2026, the Government approved increased MSPs for all mandated Rabi crops for the
Rabi Marketing Season (RMS) 2027-28
, with an estimated
₹
90,962 crore
to be paid to farmers for 324 lakh metric tonnes (MT) of produce. The expanding scale of MSP support is reflected in procurement trends and payments over the years. Procurement of six Rabi crops increased from 2,302 lakh metric tonnes (LMT) during 2004-05 to 2013-14 to 3,921 LMT during 2014-15 to 2025-26. Correspondingly,
MSP payments
rose from
₹
2.65 lakh crore to
₹
8.36 lakh crore
. Meanwhile, digital platforms are enhancing the accessibility and transparency of procurement and payment processes. Together, price assurance, expanded procurement and technology-enabled delivery are strengthening farmers’ access to markets and supporting greater confidence in agricultural decisions.
Minimum Support Price: Supporting Farmers Through Price Stability
A farmer’s economic returns are shaped not only by agricultural production but also by the prices received for the harvested produce. After investing months of labour, resources, and inputs in cultivation, the market price ultimately influences farm earnings and the capacity to sustain agricultural operations. For small and marginal farmers, adverse fluctuations in market prices can introduce considerable uncertainty into farm income and affect decisions regarding future cultivation.
In this context, the Minimum Support Price (MSP) serves as an important policy instrument for supporting farmers. It provides a price assurance mechanism through which the government undertakes procurement of eligible agricultural produce at predetermined prices. MSP ensures remunerative returns to farmers while encouraging agricultural investment and production.
By providing a measure of price assurance, MSP can help mitigate farmers’ exposure to adverse market fluctuations. When market prices are low, procurement at MSP provides an avenue to sell eligible produce at the announced price. This mechanism helps reduce price uncertainty, support farm income stability, and facilitate planning for subsequent agricultural seasons. By strengthening confidence in expected returns, MSP also contributes to farmers’ decisions regarding investment in improved seeds, agricultural technology, and other productivity-enhancing inputs.
When Better Farming Meets Assured Returns
The experience of
Shri K. Chikkana, a 72-year-old millet farmer
from Bombrahalli village, Karnataka, illustrates how improved agricultural practices, institutional support, and price assurance can contribute to enhanced farm productivity and income.
For several years, Shri Chikkana
cultivated traditional finger millet varieties
using
conventional farming methods
. Under irrigated conditions, the
productivity
remained at
around 9-11 quintals per acre
.
A significant change came during the Rabi Season of 2025, when he adopted the
improved HR-13 finger millet variety
. ICAR-IIMR (Indian Council of Agricultural Research-Indian Institute of Millets Research) supplied the variety through Kusumagiri Farmers Producer Organization, Kundrupi.
With technical guidance from ICAR-IIMR scientists, he also incorporated improved cultivation practices, including transplanting, balanced nutrient management, and natural farming approaches. These interventions helped increase his
productivity to 22-23 quintals per acre, more than doubling his earlier yield.
The productivity gains were complemented by assured procurement through the FPO at the Minimum Support Price (MSP) of
₹
4,886 per quintal (2025–26 season).
This enabled him to access remunerative prices for his produce and realise higher returns. Consequently, his income from six acres increased from approximately ₹2.07 lakh to
₹
6.59 lakh.
Shri Chikkana’s experience demonstrates how the convergence of improved seed varieties, scientific cultivation practices, technical guidance, farmer collectives, and MSP-based procurement can strengthen farm productivity and economic returns.
How Minimum Support Prices Are Determined
The government announces
Minimum Support Prices (MSPs) annually for 22 mandated agricultural crops
. These MSPs are based on recommendations from the
Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP)
. The recommendations consider the views of concerned
State Governments and Central Ministries/Departments
. Additionally, MSP for Toria and de-husked coconut are determined based on the MSPs announced for rapeseed and mustard, and copra, respectively.
The CACP considers
several factors while recommending MSPs
for different crops. These include:
cost of production
demand and supply of crops in domestic and global markets
domestic and international prices
inter-crop price parity
terms of trade between agriculture and non-agriculture sectors
likely impact of price policy on the wider economy, and
a minimum margin of
50 percent over the cost of production
.
The cost of production used in MSP calculations includes paid-out expenses on hired human, bullock and machine labour, leased-in land, seeds, fertilisers, manure, and irrigation. It also accounts for diesel and electricity used to operate pump sets, depreciation on farm implements and buildings, interest on working capital, and other miscellaneous expenses. Additionally, the imputed value of family labour is included to recognise the contribution of family members engaged in agricultural activities. The same cost-estimation formula is applied
uniformly across all 22 mandated crops
and across States for calculating MSPs.
Rabi MSP 2027-28: Price Support and Crop Diversification

on 30 September 2026.

Ensuring Accessible and Transparent MSP Procurement
The procurement process has evolved to make MSP benefits more direct, transparent, and accessible to farmers. For
cereals and coarse cereals
, the Government undertakes procurement through the
Food Corporation of India (FCI)
and designated State agencies. This provides price support to farmers at the announced MSP.
Procurement of
pulses, oilseeds and copra
is undertaken under the
Price Support Scheme (PSS)
of the Pradhan Mantri Annadata Aay Sanrakshan Abhiyan (PM-AASHA). State Governments may request procurement when prevailing market prices fall below the announced MSP. The National Agricultural Cooperative Marketing Federation of India Ltd.
(NAFED)
and the National Co-operative Consumers’ Federation of India Ltd.
(NCCF)
are key agencies responsible for undertaking procurement under the scheme. To promote domestic pulse production and strengthen self-reliance, tur, urad and masur are procured from pre-registered farmers through Central Nodal Agencies under the
Mission for Aatmanirbharta in Pulses till 2030-31.
Pradhan Mantri Annadata Aay Sanrakshan Abhiyan (PM-AASHA)
Launched in September 2018, the scheme ensures remunerative prices for farmers while maintaining price stability for consumers. One of the key components is the
Price Support Scheme (PSS)
. It is activated when market prices of
notified pulses, oilseeds, and copra
fall below MSP during peak harvest. Eligible produce meeting
Fair Average Quality
(FAQ) standards is procured
directly from pre-registered farmers possessing valid land records
via
NAFED
and
NCCF.
This eliminates intermediaries and safeguards farmers from distress sales.
To improve farmers’ access to procurement facilities, adequate numbers of procurement centres are established, with State Governments and procurement agencies publicising procurement schedules, centre locations and
Fair Average Quality (FAQ)
specifications for eligible produce.
The procurement process has also been strengthened through digital platforms. Under the Price Support Scheme (PSS), NAFED’s
e-Samriddhi
and NCCF’s
e-Samyukti
platforms facilitate key stages of procurement, including farmer registration, produce procurement and payment. Farmers register by providing details such as Aadhaar, land records, bank account information, and crop particulars. Registered farmers can select their nearest procurement centre, following which the portal schedules their visit for a specified date. Direct transfer of MSP payments to farmers’ bank accounts helps reduce manual intervention, reliance on intermediaries, and payment delays.
As on
19 October 2026
, the e-Samyukti platform has facilitated procurement involving more than
43 lakh farmers,
with
over 37.45 lakh metric tonnes
procured and more than
₹
13,000 crore
credited to farmers. Meanwhile, e-Samriddhi recorded more than
1.37crore
registered farmers, over
2.25 crore units
of produce procured, and
81+ lakh payouts
to farmers.
Further strengthening transparency and beneficiary verification, biometric authentication of farmers became mandatory under PSS from the 2025–26 season. Authentication is conducted through
Aadhaar-enabled Point of Sale (PoS)
machines or facial authentication before procurement. This measure helps verify farmer identity and ensures that procurement benefits reach
genuine and eligible beneficiaries.
The Expanding Scale of Procurement and MSP Payments to Farmers
The role of MSP in supporting agricultural procurement is reflected in the substantial increase in both procurement volumes and payments to farmers over the years. During
2014-15 to 2025-26
, wheat procurement totalled
3,715 lakh metric tonnes (LMT),
compared with
2,254 LMT
during 2004-05 to 2013-14. Similarly, procurement across six rabi crops increased to
3,921 LMT
from
2,302 LMT
over the corresponding periods.
This growth in procurement has been accompanied by a significant rise in MSP payments to farmers. Between 2014-15 and 2025-26, payments to wheat farmers amounted to
₹
7.31 lakh crore
, compared with
₹
2.56 lakh crore
during 2004-05 to 2013-14. For the six rabi crops, cumulative MSP payments increased to
₹
8.36 lakh crore
, up from
₹
2.65 lakh crore
during the earlier period.
In Rabi Marketing Season (RMS) 2026-27, wheat procurement stood at
357.57 LMT
, with an MSP value of
₹
92,432.51 crore
, benefiting over
34 lakh farmers
. These figures reflect the scale of government procurement and the financial support extended to farmers through MSP.
Supporting Farmers, Strengthening Agriculture
Minimum Support Price (MSP)
remains an important policy instrument for supporting farmers against market price fluctuations and providing greater assurance in agricultural planning and investment. The MSP decisions for
Rabi Marketing Season (RMS) 2027-28
continue to provide for a
minimum margin of 50 percent
over the cost of production.
The sustained growth in
procurement volumes and MSP payments
reflects the expanding scale of government support to farmers. Meanwhile, digital registration, biometric authentication and direct bank transfers are strengthening the accessibility and transparency of procurement processes. Overall, these measures reinforce the link between price assurance, market access and remunerative returns, supporting farmers’ income prospects and contributing to a more resilient agricultural sector.

title: NHRC, India takes suo motu cognizance of the reported parading of three persons in a semi-nude condition by police in Kolkata, West Bengal
subtitle: Issues a notice to the Kolkata Police Commissioner, calling for a detailed report on the matter within two weeks
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                29 OCT 2026 3:51PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), India has taken
suo motu
cognizance of a media report that the police paraded three persons in a semi-nude condition with ropes tied around their waists in Kolkata, West Bengal. A day before the incident, an 18-year-old youth and his 19-year-old friend, who were reportedly seen with a minor girl, were beaten and humiliated by the girl’s family members at her house. The youth’s father, whom the girl’s family summoned, was also assaulted. Subsequently, all three were stripped and forced to walk naked on the road at gunpoint.
The Commission has observed that the contents of the news report, if true, raise serious issues of violation of human rights. Therefore, it has issued a notice to the Kolkata Police Commissioner, calling for a detailed report on the matter within two weeks.
According to the media report, carried on 28th October 2026, the police brought three arrested persons, including the girl’s father, her maternal uncle and his friend, to the same locality and made them walk shirtless and barefoot for over 100 metres purportedly for reconstruction of the crime scene.

title: Department of Fertilizers and Its PSUs Make Significant Progress under Special Campaign 6
subtitle:
67,635 Sq. Ft. of Office Space Freed Through Campaign Activities

Significant Progress in File Review, Record Weeding, Scrap Disposal and Cleanliness Drives
ministry: Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers :Department of Fertilizers
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                29 OCT 2026 6:25PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Department of Fertilizers (DoF), along with its attached offices and Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs), is actively implementing
Special Campaign 6 from 2 October to 31 October 2026
. The campaign aims to institutionalize Swachhata, reduce pendency and enhance efficiency in government offices, in accordance with the guidelines issued by the Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances (DARPG).
As of 29 October 2026, the Department and its PSUs have made significant progress in reviewing physical files and e-files, weeding out old records, disposing of scrap materials and improving cleanliness in office premises. The campaign also focuses on the disposal of public grievances, appeals and other pending matters.
Key Achievements as of 29 October 2026
The Department and its PSUs have recorded the following achievements under the Special Campaign 6:
Review of Physical Files:
8,625 files reviewed out of 10,805 files identified for review.
E-File Management:
658 e-files reviewed and 345 e-files closed.
Weeding Out of Records:
1,606 physical files weeded out of 2,561 files identified for weeding.
Cleanliness Drives:
3137 outdoor cleanliness campaigns conducted by PSUs.
Scrap Disposal:
Revenue of ₹2,76,776 generated through the disposal of office scrap.
Space Freed:
67,635 square feet of space freed, enabling better utilisation of office premises.
Public Grievance Appeals:
All five public grievance appeals reported in the campaign data have been disposed of.
Simplification of Rules:
One initiative for easing of rules reported by the Department.
Social Media Outreach
As part of Special Campaign 6, the Department has published
85 social media posts
to raise awareness about cleanliness and efficient office management. These posts have been disseminated through X (Twitter), Facebook, Instagram, the WhatsApp Channel and the PIB X handle. The posts highlight cleanliness drives, records management, proper disposal of e-waste and scrap, and other campaign-related activities.
Special Campaign 6 to Continue Till 31 October 2026
Special Campaign 6 is currently underway and will continue until 31st October 2026. The Department of Fertilizers and its PSUs remain committed to sustaining cleanliness, reducing pendency, improving workplace efficiency and ensuring the proper disposal of obsolete records, e-waste and scrap materials.
The campaign reflects the Government of India's commitment to institutionalising Swachhata, promoting efficient governance and creating cleaner, more organised and productive government workplaces.
